slides.label: Lecture Map
slides.notes: Open by separating the object from its chart picture. A projective quadric is an equation class in homogeneous coordinates, while every drawn oval, pair of arcs, or ruled surface is a chart reading of that class. The lecture will keep three ledgers visible: matrix invariants, incidence data, and dual hyperplanes.

slides.label: Projective Equation
slides.notes: Use this slide to make scaling harmless. Multiplying the vector representative changes the quadratic value by a square, and multiplying the matrix representative changes the equation by a nonzero scalar. Therefore the zero condition survives both choices. Students should hear that projective geometry begins by asking which formulas are independent of representatives.

slides.label: Rank And Signature
slides.notes: The gallery is deliberately chart-level evidence, not a complete classification theorem. Ask students to read each panel twice: first as an affine picture, then as a matrix diagnosis. Rank detects degeneracy, while signature records whether real isotropic directions exist and how the chosen chart cuts them.

slides.label: Pencils
slides.notes: Present a pencil as geometry in the space of equations. The base locus lives in the original projective space, but the discriminant lives in the parameter line of matrices. The same four base points can be fixed while the determinant decides which members become singular. Keeping those spaces separate prevents many pencil mistakes.

slides.label: Ruled Quadrics
slides.notes: This is the moment to make a curved drawing feel linear. On the quadric xy minus zw equals zero, fixing one parameter gives an entire projective line, and fixing the other gives a second family. The affine surface bends, but each ruling is a genuine straight line contained in the quadric.

slides.label: Polarity
slides.notes: Move slowly from matrix multiplication to geometry. For a proper quadric, A sends a point representative to coefficients of a hyperplane. When the point lies on the quadric, the hyperplane is tangent there; when the point is external to a real conic, the polar line joins the two contact points from the point.

slides.label: Tangential Quadric
slides.notes: The dual conic should not feel like a new object invented after the fact. It is the same tangent family viewed in the dual projective plane. A hyperplane coefficient vector is tangent precisely when it satisfies the inverse-matrix equation. The visual pair lets students compare the envelope of lines with the locus of their coefficients.

slides.label: Projective Action
slides.notes: Emphasize the direction reversal in the formula. Points move by H, while equations move by the inverse transpose so that the truth of the quadratic equation is preserved. The figure verifies this with sample points: after transforming the conic, the moved samples still satisfy the moved equation up to numerical tolerance.

slides.label: Classification Ledger
slides.notes: This ledger gathers the lecture vocabulary into decisions students can actually use. The first question is whether the matrix is singular. The second is whether the real signature has both signs. The third is whether dimension and chart choice reveal topology, points at infinity, or line rulings that a single affine drawing may hide.

slides.label: Design Workflow
slides.notes: Use the workflow as an applied lab rather than a recipe to memorize. Incidence constraints are linear in the entries of A, tangency constraints come from A times x, and a remaining pencil should be checked by its determinant before drawing. The lesson is to design projectively first and choose a chart last.

slides.label: Notebook Certificate
slides.notes: The numbers here are small because they are residuals, not because the concepts are small. Each check protects a projective statement from an affine drawing error: scale invariance, base-point incidence, degenerate pencil roots, polarity contact, dual tangency, ruled-line containment, and contragredient coordinate change all pass with near machine precision.

slides.label: Recap Exercise
slides.notes: Close by making students choose the right ledger for a new quadric. They should identify the matrix class, decide whether rank and signature explain the visible chart, check whether polarity is available, and say which statement would remain true after a projective change of coordinates. That is the chapter habit in miniature.
